summary.en-US: Iliad account balance, renewal date, options and voicemail, without the carrier's site

description.en-US:
daili is an unofficial client for your Iliad mobile account: balance, renewal date,
consumption and voicemail, read the same way the carrier's own customer area shows them —
without opening a browser and logging in again.

Not affiliated with, authorised, sponsored or promoted by Iliad or any other carrier. It reads
the same pages you would reach yourself, with your own credentials, and it does not replace
the carrier's site, which stays the reference if something looks wrong.

What it shows: account credit and the current offer, renewal date, remaining calls/SMS/data
split Italy and abroad, recent calls and messages, options and voice services, voicemail you
can listen to and share without dialling into the carrier's menu, home-screen widgets, and
more than one account at once.

This build has no Google Play Billing and no Firebase in it.
This build sends two things to the developer's own server:
crash reports, and a count of installs and updates. Nothing goes to Google, and no analytics
company is involved. Both are on by default, are explained on the first launch before anything
is sent, and can be turned off there or in Settings. The privacy policy has the details.
Apart from those two, what leaves the device leaves because you sent it.

Every feature is unlocked; if daili is
useful to you, the donation reminder in it — once a week, silenceable in two taps — is what
keeps it maintained.

Your carrier credentials are encrypted on the phone with a key generated and held by Android
itself, sent only to your carrier's own site to sign you in, and never saved in any cloud:
Android's own backup is switched off for the whole app. Apart from the crash reports and the
install count above, there is no daili server.

summary.en-US: Chord sheets that scroll themselves, for the whole band

description.en-US:
bandcue puts a chord sheet on a screen on a stage: cached, scrolling by itself at the speed
of the song, with the same sheet in every hand in the band.

A guitarist on a stage has both hands busy and a phone on a stand. A browser tab needs a
signal that a basement rehearsal room, a club with a metal roof and a festival field do not
have; a PDF never scrolls itself; and paper is fine until there are forty songs and a wind.
Underneath all three, the band is not on the same version: somebody transposed the song down
a tone on Tuesday and two of the four still have the old key on Saturday.

So: the songs live on the device and open with the radios off. The scroll is continuous and
set in the unit a musician actually knows — how long the song is — so it survives a change
of font size, a rotation and a transposition that reflows a line. And the band's book is one
file per song in a folder the band already syncs, in ChordPro any other app can read.

A band shares a library rather than a room: the Band tab lists the bands you are in, and
opening a song from one asks whether you are playing it together. Everybody else's phone
tunes in on its own and scrolls with you, and whoever starts chooses whether they alone may
move it or anybody in the band can.

**bandcue never fetches a chord sheet on its own.** Songs get in because you put them there:
typed, pasted, opened from a file, shared from your own browser, or found through the search
the app runs *for you and at your request*, where you read the result and decide whether to
keep it. There is no catalogue in here, nothing to browse, and no song of anybody else's
waiting to be found.

**This build has no Google libraries in it at all** — no Play Billing and no Firebase.
This build sends two things to the developer's own server:
crash reports, and a count of installs and updates. Nothing goes to Google, and no analytics
company is involved. Both are on by default, are explained on the first launch before anything
is sent, and can be turned off there or in Settings. The privacy policy has the details.

Everything that stays on your phone is free and unlimited, and what is asked for in return is a
donation, once a week, on a notification channel that can be silenced in two taps. Your cloud
library and starting a band run on bandcue's server and need a subscription or a licence, which
a donation does not give; joining somebody else's band is free.

It is published here as a beta, ahead of the stable on Google Play.

summary.en-US: Turns an Android bug report into what to fix

description.en-US:
batbrief reads a bug report off your phone and tells you what is draining the
battery — not as a wall of graphs, but as conclusions you can act on.

Feed it a bugreport.zip (Developer options → Bug report → Full report → Share) and
every screen answers the same question in three parts: a claim, the numbers behind
it, and the setting that acts on it.

It works from the coulomb counter rather than the battery percentage, so it can tell
you how much of the drain happened while you were not using the phone — which is
where nearly all of the recoverable charge is — whether the idle drain is the same
day and night, whether the phone ever actually slept, and if it did not, whether an
app held a wakelock or the hardware kept waking the CPU. It also reports what was
downloaded in the background, what scanned continuously, which app ran a storm of
jobs, and how much capacity the battery has left.

It reads an already unzipped bug report too, and a plain
`adb shell dumpsys batterystats` dump, which Battery Historian cannot read at all.

Your bug report never leaves the phone. It is unpacked into the app\'s own cache,
analysed there, and deleted when you close it; nothing in the app sends one anywhere.
Apart from one read-only fetch of the public supporters list, which carries no identifier,
the only network requests this build makes are the two below.

This build sends two things to the developer's own server:
crash reports, and a count of installs and updates. Nothing goes to Google, and no analytics
company is involved. Both are on by default, are explained on the first launch before anything
is sent, and can be turned off there or in Settings. The privacy policy has the details.

batbrief has a paid tier — automatic capture and analysis on a schedule you set, a
personal baseline, and before/after comparisons. It cannot be bought in this build:
there is no store client here. If you bought it in the Play version, it stays
unlocked.

summary.en-US: Your machines on one screen: status, Wake-on-LAN, KVM, and SSH built for tmux.

description.en-US:
consolet puts every machine you own on one screen: whether it is on, how busy it is, a way to wake it, its physical screen and a shell. A machine is one card, however you reach it: the KVM when it is off or broken, SSH when it is up. It is made for homelabs and for machines you are not sitting at, on mobile data, through a VPN such as Tailscale.

IS IT ON, AND HOW BUSY

CPU, memory and network of a Linux machine, read over SSH with nothing to install. Windows reports through the consolet command-line tool.

WAKE IT FROM ANYWHERE

A magic packet cannot cross a VPN, so each machine has a wake route, tried in the order you choose: its own KVM, another always-on machine on its network such as a NAS or a router, or this phone on the same Wi-Fi. You see the route in use; if nothing answers, the app offers the next.

ITS PHYSICAL SCREEN

PiKVM and JetKVM open in the app through their web interface, so a machine that will not boot is still reachable. A PiKVM card also shows a preview of the screen and the real power light, and can switch the machine on and off where ATX is wired.

A TERMINAL MADE FOR TMUX AND BYOBU

The app knows whether it is looking at tmux, byobu or a plain shell. Sessions appear as a list. Windows are real tabs: tap, swipe, long-press to rename or close.

KEYS THAT FOLLOW WHAT IS RUNNING

The bar above the keyboard follows the context: byobu's F2, F3 and F4, the same actions as prefix sequences under tmux, latching ctrl and alt in a shell, and every set can be changed. A real text field above the keys keeps your keyboard's swipe, autocorrect and voice typing and sends a long prompt as one paste; with an agent such as Claude Code, tapping the terminal opens it.

FOR CLAUDE CODE

When Claude Code asks you to run a command or open a link, it is already on your clipboard, even one split across lines. A permission question becomes a card with big buttons. Nothing ever runs by itself: a command still waits for your enter. While a session is open, a notification tells you Claude is waiting; with no push service, nothing arrives when the app is not connected.

THE PASSWORDS YOU TYPE EVERY TIME

Save a machine's disk or login password. They stay encrypted on your phone (except a KVM login you send to your relay) and, with your fingerprint, consolet types them through the KVM or into a LUKS unlock prompt over SSH. You watch the screen and you press enter.

THE COMMAND-LINE TOOL AND THE RELAY

consolet is also one small, optional program for Linux and Windows, fit for a NAS or a router. Over SSH, with no daemon and no account, it sends the wake packet from that network, lists what is on it and reports a machine's status. As consolet relay, on an always-on Linux machine at home, it watches that home's machines all the time: paired once, over an end-to-end encrypted channel, the app finds it on your Wi-Fi and reads its cards from it at home, over your tailnet or, with Pro, through our server, which sees who connects but cannot read the sealed channel. Wake, Reboot and Shut down go through it. It reads your KVMs too (a PiKVM's lights and picture, a JetKVM's DC reading) and presses a PiKVM's ATX. A KVM login you agree to send reaches it sealed; it can open it. It links to our server only when needed; --no-backend stops that.

SYNC BETWEEN YOUR PHONES (PRO)

Off until you turn it on. It keeps your machines, their host keys and your vault of keys and passwords the same on every phone you add, end-to-end encrypted: everything is sealed on your phone, and the server keeps only what it cannot read. Nobody can recover your passphrase or recovery code for you.

YOUR MACHINES STAY YOURS

You need no account to use consolet; your machines, hosts, keys, passwords and sessions reach no service of ours in a form it can read. An account (an emailed code) is needed only for sync and to read the answers to your reports. No ads, no tracking.

This build contains no Google Play services and no Firebase: it sends no crash reports and no usage statistics.

consolet is an independent app, not affiliated with PiKVM, JetKVM, Tailscale or Anthropic.

summary.en-US: Turns Private DNS off while a VPN is up, and back on after

description.en-US:
Android's Private DNS and a VPN do not get along: bring the tunnel up and name resolution
stops behaving — internal names go unresolved, and the setting that fixes it is turning
Private DNS off. Turn it off and forget, and your DNS is in the clear on the next café Wi-Fi.

dnsetter watches for the VPN and switches Private DNS off while it is up, then puts it back
exactly as it was — hostname included — when the VPN goes away. Set your phone down and it
keeps doing that; change Private DNS by hand while the tunnel is up and it takes that as your
new intent and stops switching.

A rule per VPN app, because not every VPN collides with Private DNS: a commercial one with its
own public resolver is perfectly happy alongside it, while a tunnel with names of its own is
not. Android does not reliably tell an ordinary app which tunnel is up, so where it does not,
dnsetter assumes the only VPN app you have installed and labels that as an assumption — and
with two installed and neither named, your default rule applies rather than a guess.

A Quick Settings tile for the times you want to decide yourself: off from the shade, tap again
and your setting comes back.

It needs one permission that no dialog can grant: WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS. There are three ways
to give it, and the app's first screen is all three: from a computer with ADB, from the phone
alone over wireless debugging, or — with no shell at all — through Shizuku, which dnsetter now
integrates. With Shizuku running it is one tap, and afterwards the app holds the permission in
its own right: Shizuku can be stopped or uninstalled and nothing changes. Until the permission
lands the app is inert and says so rather than pretending to work.

It never creates a VPN of its own, since Android allows one at a time and taking it would
defeat the point. Every change it makes is read back before it is reported, because some
manufacturer skins quietly ignore the write, and an app that claims a switch it did not make
leaves you resolving in the clear believing you are not.

Your DNS, your VPN, your rules and your settings are not among the things the app sends. It
asks for internet access for three things: the report screen and the messages screen under
Info, which send what you type, when you press send; and
the crash reports and install count described next. The first beta declared no internet
permission at all; that is what changed.

This build sends two things to the developer's own server:
crash reports, and a count of installs and updates. Nothing goes to Google, and no analytics
company is involved. Both are on by default, are explained on the first launch before anything
is sent, and can be turned off there or in Settings. The privacy policy has the details.

A crash report never contains logs, anything you wrote or stored in the app, or location. An
error message could still mention something the app was handling, which is why messages are
masked before they are sent.

There is no paywall in this build. Every feature is open, including the per-VPN rules that are
Pro on Google Play, and what is asked instead is a donation — once a week, on a notification
you can silence in two taps, which takes nothing away because nothing was held back.

This is a beta. The collision it exists for is documented nowhere by Google: it is a
first-hand observation on one phone with one tunnel, and this build has not yet been run
against any other. That is what the beta is for.

summary.en-US: A compass that says how much to believe it

description.en-US:
fastcompass is being built towards one idea: a number is worth nothing without where it came
from and how much to trust it. **The compass is built; the altitude and the satellite view are
not.**

What it does today:

* A compass that shows which way you are facing, which sensor the heading came from, and how
  much of it to believe. A magnetic compass is wrong indoors, in a car and next to anything
  magnetic, and the phone knows it — the sensor reports its own accuracy, that accuracy is part
  of the dial, and when the sensor declares itself unreliable **the needle stops** rather than
  pointing confidently at nothing.
* It says magnetic north, and says so, because it does not yet correct for declination.
* A way to write in and read the answer.

What it does NOT do yet:

* **No altitude.** The tab states what it will be and measures nothing. Getting it right means
  correcting the GPS height, which is measured against a mathematical model of the Earth rather
  than sea level — some 45 to 50 metres out in Italy — and most apps print it anyway.
* **No satellite view.** Which constellations are overhead and which are in the fix is the
  screen that explains a poor position, and it is not built.
* **No true north**, and **no heading from your movement across the ground** for when you are
  moving faster than walking pace. Both need a position, and nothing here reads one yet.

The app declares the permissions those features will need and uses none of them today.

No account.

summary.en-US: Follow a flight — in progress: no data provider is wired up yet

description.en-US:
flighter is being built for the person meeting somebody at arrivals rather than for someone
watching aviation: the two or three flights you actually care about, and a word the moment one
changes. **This version has no flight data provider, so it looks up no flights.**

What it does today:

* The shape of the app: add a flight by number and date, keep a small list of them, and see
  for each one which polling rate it would be on and what that would cost in requests.
* Says on the screen that no source is configured, rather than showing an invented gate.
* A way to write in and read the answer.

What it does NOT do yet, and why:

* **No flight status of any kind** — no delay, no gate, no boarding, no landing. Aviation data
  is bought per request and the provider has not been chosen: the candidates differ by an order
  of magnitude in price and in European coverage, and a client written against documentation
  nobody has called is fiction that compiles. It arrives with a key and a saved real response.
* **No notifications**, for the same reason.

What is already decided and already in the code is the part that is hard to retrofit: four
times kept apart and never blended — scheduled, estimated, actual, and absent — every fact
carrying its age, and a polling ladder written against the free tier's request budget rather
than against a clock, with the rung it is on shown in words.

No account, and no location permission of any kind: an app about somebody else's flight has no
reason to know where you are.

summary.en-US: Write down what you spend and see how much of your budgets is left

description.en-US:
hello-budget writes down what you spend and tells you how much of your budgets is left, this
month, right now. It is the Android app of the Hello Budget bot on Telegram: sign in with
Telegram and everything you wrote down in the bot is already here, and what you write here is in
the bot a second later.

An expense is an amount, a category and a date. The amount screen is a calculator; a purchase
can be spread over months; an expense can be refunded. Budgets are ceilings on categories, monthly,
quarterly, yearly or one-off, and the summary shows what is left of each. Income, subscriptions
and instalments, shared accounts with a percentage each, investments with their cost and gain,
search, charts, CSV export and import, and deleting your data or your account are all in the
app, in Italian and English.

The data is on the Hello Budget server and is the same as the bot's, the Mini App's and the
web app's. **This build has no Google libraries in it at all**: no Play Billing, no Firebase,
so no crash reporting and no usage statistics, gated or otherwise. You can sign in with
Telegram or with a code sent to your email; an email you linked in the bot opens the bot's
account.

Hello Budget has a paid tier, Pro: no limits, subscriptions, charts, export and the monthly
backup. It cannot be bought inside this app: there is no store client here. It is bought in the
Hello Budget bot on Telegram, and if you already have Pro on your account this app shows it
and unlocks everything.

summary.en-US: What's in your pantry, fridge and freezer, with expiry dates under control

description.en-US:
hello-pantry keeps track of what you have at home (the cupboard, the fridge, the freezer) and
shows you what is about to expire before it does. It is the Android app of Hello Pantry: sign in
with the account you already use in the Telegram bot or in the web app, and your homes and
everything in them are already there.

* Your home, place by place. Every product sits in a place (fridge, freezer, cupboard, whatever
  you call them), with how much of it you have and when it expires.
* Scan to add. Point the camera at a barcode: if the product is already in your home you add
  another one; if Hello Pantry's shared catalog or Open Food Facts knows it, the name is filled
  in for you to check. No barcode? Add it by name. Scanning runs on the device, with ZXing.
* Quick add. Your recent products are one tap away, with where, how many and the expiry of the
  last time already proposed; or write it the way you would say it, like "2 milk 1l 12/11", and
  the number of packages, the size and the expiry are filled in for you to check.
* Photos. Take a photo of a package or pick one from the gallery; it is shrunk on the phone
  before it is sent.
* The shared catalog. A product nobody knew can go into Hello Pantry's shared catalog with its
  photo; you can report a wrong or offensive entry and correct the ones you added. You can also
  send a new product to Open Food Facts, a choice you make every time, and see what became of it
  in Contributions.
* Eaten or thrown away. Mark what you used, a whole pack or just part of it, and whether it was
  eaten or wasted. Changed your mind? Undo it.
* Expiring soon. One list of what expires next, soonest first.
* Expiry alerts on the phone. A notification before your products expire, one per home, at the
  hour you set for it. The phone works it out by itself every hour, with no Google services and
  no connection needed. If you also use the Hello Pantry bot, you choose where alerts arrive: on
  the phone or on Telegram.
* Shopping list. What runs low goes on the list; tick it off once you have bought it.
* Statistics. How much you eat and how much you throw away, by month, year or since the start:
  the share that goes in the bin, what expired at home, the last six months, and by person.
* People and news. Invite the people you live with by their Telegram username, give each a role
  (owner, editor or viewer), and choose when the Telegram bot tells you what the others do, and about whom.
* Your data. The owner of a home can export it as a file; anyone can delete all their data from
  the app.
* Signing in, and your account. With a code sent to your email, or with a code from the Hello
  Pantry bot on Telegram. One account for the bot, the web app and this app. In Settings,
  Account, you can link Telegram with a code from the bot and add or change your sign-in email;
  when the other account already exists the app tells you what happens, and two accounts that
  both have data are never merged. A short welcome tour comes once, after your first sign-in.

Free and Pro: free is one home with one place and a limited number of products, with scanning,
expiry dates and the shopping list. Pro belongs to your account, so it holds in the bot, in the
web app and here: no limits on homes, places and products. The app does not sell it and has no
payment of any kind; in this build, Pro is turned on from the Telegram bot.

This build contains no Google Play services and no Firebase: nothing in it reports anything on
its own. The app talks to Hello Pantry's own server (your account and your pantry) and to Open
Food Facts for product names.

Product names and photos come in part from Open Food Facts, available under the Open Database
License.

summary.en-US: What is in Italian cinemas, and a watchlist that tracks undated films

description.en-US:
movier is being built towards one question: what is on at the cinema near you tonight, and is
any of it in the original language. This early version answers the half of that question which
can be answered honestly today.

What it does:

* What is on release in Italy right now, with posters, synopses and the original title beside
  the Italian one — because the original title is the name a versione originale listing uses.
* A screen per film: synopsis, runtime, original language, and the Italian cinema release date
  rather than the international one.
* Search any film by title, in Italian or in the original.
* A watchlist, kept on the device, grouped into what is in cinemas now, what is announced, and
  what has no date yet. That last group is the one no listings site keeps.

What it does NOT do yet, and why:

* **There are no showtimes.** No cinemas, no times, no original-language filter. Those need a
  listings source, and there is no free, public, legal API for Italian cinema listings — every
  one that exists is commercial and quote-based. Rather than scrape a portal or ship a screen
  that guesses, the app says so on its first screen and leaves those tabs empty.

So this version is useful if you follow films and want to know what has opened here; it is not
yet the app that finds you a VO screening on a Tuesday. That is the next thing, and it depends
on a licence rather than on code.

No account, no personalised feed, no trailers, and no notification that was not asked for by
name. Film data and posters come from The Movie Database (TMDB), credited in the app under
Info; this product uses the TMDB API but is not endorsed or certified by TMDB.

summary.en-US: Search your indexers and play from your TorBox account

description.en-US:
ondalet searches the engines and torrent sites you set up and plays what is in your TorBox
account. It is a beta.

It comes with no content, no TorBox account and no indexer: you need your own TorBox account,
your own Newznab, Torznab or Prowlarr indexers, or both.

What it does:

* **Search.** Your Newznab, Torznab and Prowlarr engines, and six public torrent sites that
  start switched off. Filters, sorting, saved searches that show what is new since the last
  run, recent searches and preview images.
* **TorBox.** Sign in with a code or a key. Results TorBox already has carry a Cached badge;
  add a result to TorBox from its page.
* **Library.** What is in your TorBox with its progress, the files of each item by season,
  and Remove.
* **Play.** In the app: video in landscape with picture in picture, audio and subtitle tracks
  (including the subtitle files of a torrent), speed, resume, Continue watching and the next
  episode; audio keeps playing in the background. Or in another player you choose.
* **Backup and restore.** Your settings in a file, encrypted with a passphrase or plain.

Not there yet: playing or downloading straight from a Usenet provider (you can set one up,
nothing uses it yet), downloading to the phone, and a Cached badge on NZB results.

This is a beta: tried on an emulator and on one real TorBox account, not yet on many phones
and files. F-Droid does not suggest it; pick it from the versions on the app's page.

Free, with no advertising. No analytics and no account of its own.

summary.en-US: A launcher for Android TV with community themes and wallpapers

description.en-US:
sofalet is a home screen for Android TV and Google TV, built to be looked at from the sofa.

What it does:

* **Community themes.** Change the whole look of the home screen with a theme written by
  someone else, or write your own.
* **Wallpapers.** Photos, or animated wallpapers that stay smooth on a television's weak GPU.
* **Colours from the wallpaper.** The accent colours follow the picture on screen and change
  with it.
* **Network status.** Wi-Fi or Ethernet, at a glance. No network name is read and no
  location permission is asked.
* **Weather.** The forecast for the city you pick, from Open-Meteo.
* **Now playing.** What is playing in your apps, with its progress.
* **Continue watching.** An optional row built from the Watch Next rows of your other apps.
* **Modules.** Other apps can add widgets and rows to the home screen. Every module is off
  until you turn it on.

Google TV does not let you choose another home screen, so sofalet offers an accessibility
service that brings it to the front when you press Home. It is never turned on for you: you
do it in the system's accessibility settings, after a screen that says exactly what it reads.

Free, with no advertising. A weekly reminder asks if you would like to make a donation; it
can be silenced.

summary.en-US: Your own music server, on your phone

description.en-US:
StarSonic plays the music you already host yourself. Point it at your Subsonic,
Navidrome or Airsonic server and it copies the catalogue onto the phone, so browsing
your library does not wait on the network — and neither does the train tunnel.

The library is a real database on the device rather than a view of the server: artists,
albums, tracks and playlists are synced in the background, through Android's own
account and sync system, so it appears under Settings → Accounts and obeys the phone's
sync and battery rules instead of inventing a scheduler.

More than one server can be configured at once. They coexist rather than being profiles
you switch between: every album knows which server it came from.

Playback is a normal Android media session, so the lock screen, the notification,
Bluetooth buttons and anything that browses media on the phone all work. It can also
cast to a Chromecast, including music already cached on the device.

No account of the author's and no server of the author's: every byte comes from a
machine you run.

THIS IS A BETA. It works, but the server it talks to is the Subsonic API — Navidrome,
Airsonic and Subsonic itself — and nothing else. Install it if you want to try it, not
to rely on it.

summary.en-US: Live icons in the status bar, without root

description.en-US:
statlet draws live values in the Android status bar — weather and temperature,
network speed, data used, GPS speed, phone temperature, battery, RAM and free
storage — on a device that has never been rooted.

It works by the one route the platform leaves open: every notification contributes
its small icon to the status bar, so each widget is an ongoing, silent notification
whose icon is a bitmap the app draws itself. One notification channel per icon, so
any single icon can be muted or hidden from the system settings.

On Android 16 and later the system bundles an app's notifications and shows one
icon for the bundle; there statlet switches to a single icon that takes turns
through the values you enabled, with all of them listed in the expanded
notification.

This build contains no Google Play Billing and no Firebase.
This build sends two things to the developer's own server:
crash reports, and a count of installs and updates. Nothing goes to Google, and no analytics
company is involved. Both are on by default, are explained on the first launch before anything
is sent, and can be turned off there or in Settings. The privacy policy has the details.
Apart from those two, what leaves the device leaves because you sent it — a bug
report, or a name for the list of the people who support the app.

The Pro features are all unlocked; if statlet is useful to you, the donation links in it are what
keeps it maintained.

summary.en-US: Syncs a phone folder with your NAS or your cloud

description.en-US:
synclet keeps a folder on the phone and a folder on a remote in step — on a schedule
you set, over whichever protocol that remote speaks.

This is an early release. It does SFTP and WebDAV, one way at a time, upload or
download, with the local end granted through the system folder picker so no storage
permission is involved.

What it does differently: a remote is not one address. The same NAS is one address on
the home Wi-Fi and another from outside, so synclet holds a list of addresses per
remote and picks the first that answers — a plain reachability probe that needs no
permission at all, rather than reading the Wi-Fi name, which on Android costs a
location permission. When no address answers, the run is postponed rather than failed:
a NAS that is not reachable from a café has not gone wrong.

It is also honest about scheduling. Android's floor for periodic work is 15 minutes
and Doze can stretch it to hours; the app says so where the interval is chosen instead
of promising a cadence the platform will not deliver.

Nothing is ever deleted, on either side, in this version — mirroring arrives with the
safeguards it needs and not one release earlier. Files modified in the last 30 seconds
are skipped, since they may still be being written, and uploads are written under a
temporary name and renamed on success, so a half-written file never appears under its
final name. An SSH host key is pinned the first time it is seen, and a change stops the
run rather than being accepted silently.

No account, no server of the author's: every byte goes from the phone to a remote you
configured.

summary.en-US: Trips across cities: stops, legs and days, each in its own time zone

description.en-US:
tourlet keeps a trip that crosses cities in one place: the stops, the flights, trains, buses
and ferries between them, and what happens on each day, every time shown in the time zone of
the place it happens in.

A trip is a sequence of stops joined by legs. The Days tab lays it out three ways: a timeline,
grouped by the place you sleep, or one compact line per thing. Mark the stop where you spend
the nights; a trip has a departure city and a return city, each with its own time zone, so the
outbound flight and the way home are timed right. Now shows what comes next, and how long until
it.

Keep lists of places you might go to, with an icon each, and put one on a day when you decide.
Plan alternative itineraries and compare them side by side. Track the planned budget against
what you actually spend, set reminders before a departure, a check-in or an activity, get an
evening summary of tomorrow, and keep four home-screen widgets. Export a trip as a calendar, a
PDF, a spreadsheet or a KML file for Google My Maps, and import a My Maps file as lists of
places.

The map of the trip and place search use OpenStreetMap data, with search by Photon.

Sign in with an address and a mailed code to accept an invitation to somebody else's trip,
which is free. Syncing your own trips, inviting people, the public link, live sharing, forwarding
booking mails, flight watching, suggestions, forecasts and real routes run on tourlet's server
and need a subscription or a licence, which a donation does not give. Picking a trip's cover
from Unsplash is free once signed in.

**This build has no Google libraries in it**: no Play Billing, no Firebase, no Google Maps and
no push notifications.

This build sends two things to the developer's own server:
crash reports, and a count of installs and updates. Nothing goes to Google, and no analytics
company is involved. Both are on by default, are explained on the first launch before anything
is sent, and can be turned off there or in Settings. The privacy policy has the details.

Everything that runs on the phone is open; what is asked for in return is a donation, once a week, on a notification
channel that can be silenced in two taps.

Android 8 and later.

summary.en-US: A radar-first weather app, in progress: the shell, nothing fetched yet

description.en-US:
weathering is being built towards a radar you can trust at a glance: what has already
happened drawn differently from what is only expected. **This version is the shell of that
app, and it fetches no weather data at all.**

What it does today:

* Opens on the radar tab, and every one of the five tabs states what it will be and what it
  knows now — which is nothing. No tile, no forecast, no alert.
* A way to write in and read the answer, which is the one part that works end to end.

What it does NOT do yet:

* **No radar.** No tiles are fetched and none are cached.
* **No forecast.** The models it will name — ECMWF, GFS, ICON, AROME — are not called.
* **No alerts.** Nothing is watched and no notification is posted.
* **No location is read**, which follows from the above rather than being a feature yet.

The design it is being built to is public and unusually specific: observed and forecast
frames never drawn alike, a nowcast and a forecast never blended into one line, the
precipitation scale left as meteorological convention rather than themed, and one
notification per event that retracts itself when the forecast it stated does not happen.
None of that is in this build. It is listed here so that the versions are somewhere and the
work is visible, not because it is ready to use.

No account, and no advertising of any kind.

This build sends two things to the developer's own server:
crash reports, and a count of installs and updates. Nothing goes to Google, and no analytics
company is involved. Both are on by default, are explained on the first launch before anything
is sent, and can be turned off there or in Settings. The privacy policy has the details.
